source.title: The Low-Rank Simplicity Bias in Deep Networks
source.authors: Minyoung Huh; H. Mobahi; Richard Zhang; Brian Cheung; Pulkit Agrawal; Phillip Isola

record.tranche_reason: The study reports training-accuracy curves for CIFAR100 models, a different measure from the claim’s explicit zero-training-error results. Its main experiments concern low-rank embeddings and least-squares regression.
record.gate_note: Figure 7 includes training-accuracy curves for original and linearly over-parameterized CNNs on CIFAR100. The text does not state their training-accuracy outcomes; other classification results report test accuracy only. Least-squares training-loss results are a different task and do not establish the claim’s classification findings.
record.test_reason: Figure 7 reports the study's own CIFAR100 CNN training accuracy under SGD. Training accuracy and training classification error are complementary measures, so this is the same method and measure relevant to V1, despite the paper's different main question. The supplied text does not preserve readable accuracy curves.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that depth biases networks toward lower-effective-rank embeddings, and that linear expansion can improve classification generalization without changing functional capacity. They also report impaired fitting of high-rank regression targets at greater depth. They do not explicitly characterize Figure 7's final CIFAR100 training accuracies.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies low-rank embedding bias and linear over-parameterization; its CIFAR classification experiments report best test accuracy and a training-accuracy plot, rather than testing the claim’s training-error outcomes across random or corrupted labels.
record.method_sensitivity: Depth and expansion factor affect effective-rank and generalization findings; the optimal expansion factor varies with model depth.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 1 and Appendix F report that deeper width-64 ReLU networks retain higher least-squares training loss on high-rank linear regression tasks, despite extended training and hyperparameter searches.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing depth can impair fitting high-rank regression targets even when shallow networks fit them perfectly.

fits_no_version.finding: Figures 3–6 and Appendix M report depth-dependent embedding rank, including zero-loss regression solutions in some settings and failure of deeper networks to fit static Gaussian noise in others.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth biases regression networks toward lower-effective-rank solutions and can prevent fitting high-rank targets or observation noise.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix I compares effective rank in linear feed-forward and residual networks, with and without batch normalization; it also reports unstable output variance in unnormalized residual networks beyond 16 layers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Identity shortcuts alter depth-dependent rank contraction in linear regression networks, while normalization affects their output stability.

fits_no_version.finding: Appendix F states that variance-controlled Kaiming initialization was critical for stabilizing linearly expanded classification networks, but supplies no comparative training-speed or maximum-trainable-depth result.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Controlling initialization variance can stabilize training of linearly expanded networks.

record.problems: For the classification training-accuracy result relevant to V1, the paper provides only a figure and does not describe the outcome in text. The reported classification table values are test accuracies, not training errors.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. The paper reports least-squares regression results, but those do not measure the classification behavior named by the claim versions.

untested.parts: CIFAR10 training classification error; corrupted or random classification labels; systematic model-size comparisons, early stopping, and regularized training-error comparisons. CIFAR100 training accuracy is measured, but its outcome is unreadable here.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems, spurious-local-minimum frequencies, and adding one or two student neurons.
Training-error degradation in plain batch-normalized CNNs and its prevention by identity shortcuts; very deep plain tanh training and Fixup.

Comparative training speed or trainable depth under activation-matched initializations, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and orthogonal convolution kernels. Initialization-dependent embedding rank and qualitative stabilization remarks do not establish these outcomes.
Learning rates relative to a measured initial stability threshold, loss recovery with falling curvature, and edge-of-stability dynamics.
Accuracy gained per training time or step and learning-rate tolerance with versus without batch normalization; Fixup comparisons.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict is justified from R1 or R2 because neither training-accuracy outcome is readable in the supplied text. Tables 1–3 report test accuracy and cannot substitute for training error. The regression findings do not challenge the specifically scoped CIFAR classification claim, and effective-rank comparisons do not establish V3 or V6.

versions.untested_parts: The study includes CIFAR100 training-accuracy curves, but does not state their outcomes in text. It does not test CIFAR10 training error, random or corrupted labels, smaller models, early stopping, or the cited comparison with Zhang et al. and Nakkiran et al.
